issues.legal_issue: Time spent prosecuting a suit in good faith before a court that could not entertain it for want of pecuniary jurisdiction is excluded when determining whether the re-presented suit challenging a father's alienation of ancestral property is within limitation.
material_facts: The alienees took possession under the sale in 1959, and the suit challenging the alienation was first filed in 1970, within twelve years of that possession.
The suit was initially filed in a court that was later found to lack pecuniary jurisdiction and was returned for presentation to the proper court.
The plaintiffs re-presented the suit in the competent court in 1975 after prosecuting it in good faith before the first court.
issues.conclusion: The suit was within limitation because the time spent prosecuting it before the court lacking pecuniary jurisdiction was excluded.
issues.legal_principle: Article 109 of the Limitation Act, 1963 provides a twelve-year limitation period for a Mitakshara Hindu's suit to set aside his father's alienation of ancestral property, running from the alienee taking possession. Section 14 permits exclusion of time spent prosecuting in good faith and with due diligence before a court unable to entertain the proceeding because of a jurisdictional defect. No earlier cases are relied on for this issue.

rule.if: ancestral_alienation_suit and initial_filing_within_limit and first_court_lacked_jurisdiction and good_faith_prosecution

predicates.ancestral_alienation_suit: A person brought a suit to challenge a father's alienation of ancestral property.
predicates.initial_filing_within_limit: The plaintiff first filed the suit before the limitation period had expired.
predicates.first_court_lacked_jurisdiction: The first court could not entertain the suit because it lacked jurisdiction.
predicates.good_faith_prosecution: The plaintiff prosecuted the suit in good faith before it was returned for presentation to a competent court.

issues.definition: When a timely suit challenging a father's alienation of ancestral property is prosecuted in good faith before a court that lacks jurisdiction, the suit remains within limitation after presentation to a competent court.

issues.legal_issue: A father's alienation of ancestral property binds his sons when it is made for family necessity or the benefit of the family and is not shown to be for an illegal or immoral purpose.
material_facts: The house was ancestral property, and the father was the manager of the joint Hindu family.
The father sold the house, which was in a dilapidated and ruinous condition, while living with his family elsewhere and earning a modest salary; the sale was recited to be for family necessity.
The purchasers made inquiries about the father's need for money before the sale.
The plaintiffs did not produce cogent evidence rebutting the recital of family necessity or show that the transaction was for an illegal or immoral purpose.
The purchasers substantially reconstructed the house after buying it, and the father stood by the sale for many years before supporting the challenge brought by his sons.
issues.conclusion: The alienation was for the benefit of the family and was binding on the plaintiffs; they were not entitled to relief, and their suit was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a father who is the manager of a joint family may alienate coparcenary property, including his sons' interests, for legal necessity or the benefit of the family. A father may also alienate it to discharge an antecedent debt, provided that the debt was not incurred for an illegal or immoral purpose. The Court referred to Mulla's Hindu Law, 16th edition, paragraphs 242 and 256. It assessed the asserted necessity in light of the sale deed's recital, the surrounding circumstances, the purchasers' inquiries, and the evidence; no earlier case was cited on this issue.

rule.if: ancestral_property_alienation_case and father_was_family_manager and family_necessity_or_benefit and no_illegal_or_immoral_purpose_shown

predicates.ancestral_property_alienation_case: Sons challenged their father's transfer of property in which they claimed interests by birth.
predicates.father_was_family_manager: The father managed the joint family when he made the transfer.
predicates.family_necessity_or_benefit: The transfer met a family need or benefited the family, as supported by the property's condition and the circumstances of the transaction.
predicates.no_illegal_or_immoral_purpose_shown: The challengers did not establish that the transfer was made for an illegal or immoral purpose.

issues.definition: When sons challenge their family manager father's transfer of ancestral property, the transfer binds them if it served family necessity or benefit and no illegal or immoral purpose is shown.
